math1-w1-q1.question: Which of these numbers is irrational?
math1-w1-q1.explanation: √7 is not the square of any integer, so its decimal neither terminates nor repeats — it is irrational. 0.333... = 1/3 and √16 = 4 are rational. 22/7 is also rational; people make the mistake of thinking it is π.

math1-w1-q2.question: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and B = {4, 5, 6, 7}. What is A − B?
math1-w1-q2.explanation: A − B contains the elements that are in A but not in B: 1, 2, 3. {6, 7} is B − A, and {4, 5} is the intersection. {1, 2, 3, 6, 7} is the symmetric difference, which is a different concept.

math1-w1-q3.question: How many subsets does the set {a, b, c, d} have in total?
math1-w1-q3.explanation: There are 4 elements, so subsets = 2⁴ = 16 (both ∅ and the full set included). 15 is the count of proper subsets — that is the trap. 8 = 2³ uses the wrong power.

math1-w1-q4.question: In a survey of 100 people, 45 read a Hindi newspaper, 60 read an English newspaper, and 20 read both. How many people read at least one newspaper?
math1-w1-q4.explanation: |H ∪ E| = 45 + 60 − 20 = 85. If you don't subtract the intersection you get 105, which is more than the total number of people. 15 is the count of people who read no newspaper.

math1-w1-q5.question: Which of these statements is correct?
options: Every rational number is an integer
Every integer is a rational number
math1-w1-q5.explanation: Any integer n can be written as n/1, so every integer is rational (ℤ ⊆ ℚ). The reverse is not true: 1/2 is rational but not an integer. √2 is irrational, and ℝ contains irrationals too, so ℝ ⊆ ℚ is false.

math1-w1-q6.question: U = {1, 2, 3, ..., 10}. A = the even numbers in U, B = the multiples of 3 in U. What is |(A ∪ B)ᶜ|?
math1-w1-q6.explanation: A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, B = {3, 6, 9}. A ∪ B = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10} — 7 elements (6 only once). Complement = {1, 5, 7}, i.e. 3. If you count 6 twice, the union looks like 8 and you get the wrong answer 2; 7 is the size of the union, not of the complement.

math1-w1-q7.question: Write the repeating decimal 0.272727... in p/q form.
math1-w1-q7.explanation: Let x = 0.2727... Two digits repeat, so 100x = 27.2727..., and 100x − x = 27, i.e. x = 27/99 = 3/11. 27/100 is 0.27, which terminates, and 3/10 = 0.3. For a repeating block, divide by 99, not 100.

math1-w1-q8.question: What is the roster form of the set {x | x ∈ ℤ, −2 < x ≤ 3}?
math1-w1-q8.explanation: −2 < x means −2 itself is not included, and x ≤ 3 means 3 is included. Integers: −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. The first option also takes −2 (the difference between < and ≤ was missed), the third leaves out 3. {0, 1, 2, 3} comes from treating x ∈ ℤ as natural numbers.

math1-w1-q9.question: Which of these expressions has a rational value?
math1-w1-q9.explanation: √2 · √18 = √36 = 6, which is rational. In √3 + 1 and √5/2, adding a rational to an irrational or dividing it by one keeps it irrational, and π/2 is irrational too. Calling something irrational just because it has a √ is the trap — simplify first.

math1-w1-q10.question: Each of the 40 students at a coaching centre takes at least one subject — Maths or Stats. 25 students take Maths and 22 take Stats. How many students take both subjects?
math1-w1-q10.explanation: Every student takes at least one subject, so |M ∪ S| = 40. Use the formula in reverse: |M ∩ S| = |M| + |S| − |M ∪ S| = 25 + 22 − 40 = 7. 47 = 25 + 22 is just the sum, which is even more than the total of 40. 3 = 25 − 22 and 15 = 40 − 25 have nothing to do with this question.

math1-w1-q11.question: U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}. What is Aᶜ ∩ B?
math1-w1-q11.explanation: Aᶜ = U − A = {5, 6, 7, 8}. Its intersection with B = {5, 6}; this is just B − A. {1, 2} is A − B (the complement of the wrong set was taken), {7, 8} is (A ∪ B)ᶜ, and {3, 4} is A ∩ B.

math1-w1-q12.question: In a class of 80 students, 48 play cricket, 35 play football, and 12 play neither game. How many students play exactly one game?
math1-w1-q12.explanation: At least one game = 80 − 12 = 68. Both = 48 + 35 − 68 = 15. Exactly one = (at least one) − (both) = 68 − 15 = 53. 68 is 'at least one', not exactly one — the students who play both are included in it. 15 is the number who play both, and in 83 = 48 + 35 the common students are counted twice.

math1-w1-q13.question: A ⊆ B, with |A| = 2 and |B| = 6. How many sets C are there such that A ⊆ C ⊆ B?
math1-w1-q13.explanation: C must contain both elements of A. Each of the remaining 6 − 2 = 4 elements of B has two choices: in C or not. So there are 2⁴ = 16 sets (C = A and C = B are both included). 64 = 2⁶ counts all subsets of B, many of which do not contain A. 15 comes from leaving out C = A or C = B.

math1-w1-q14.question: The universal set U has 40 elements. A ⊆ U has 28 elements and B ⊆ U has 20 elements. What is the minimum possible value of |A ∩ B|?
math1-w1-q14.explanation: |A ∪ B| = 28 + 20 − |A ∩ B|, and A ∪ B lies inside U, so |A ∪ B| ≤ 40. Hence 48 − |A ∩ B| ≤ 40, i.e. |A ∩ B| ≥ 8; exactly 8 is reached when A ∪ B = U. 0 is impossible, because the union would then be 48, more than 40. 20 is the maximum possible value (when B ⊆ A), not the minimum.

math1-w1-q15.question: Of the numbers √9, 0.1010010001... (one more zero each time), 3.14, √12/√3, π − 1 and √2 + √8, how many are irrational?
math1-w1-q15.explanation: √9 = 3, 3.14 = 314/100 and √12/√3 = √4 = 2 — all three are rational. In 0.1010010001... the block of zeros keeps growing, so the decimal never repeats: irrational. π − 1 is irrational, and √2 + √8 = √2 + 2√2 = 3√2 is irrational too. Total 3. Treating 3.14 as π or not simplifying √12/√3 leads to 4 or 5.

math1-w2-q1.question: A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y, z}. What is |A × B|?
math1-w2-q1.explanation: |A × B| = |A| · |B| = 2 · 3 = 6 ordered pairs. 5 comes from mistakenly adding the sizes — for a product you have to multiply.

math1-w2-q2.question: Which of these relations from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b} is NOT a function?
math1-w2-q2.explanation: In the third option, input 1 has two outputs (a and b), so it is not a function. The first option is also a valid function — all inputs having the same output is allowed, as long as each input has only one output.

math1-w2-q3.question: Relation R on ℤ: a R b if (a − b) is divisible by 5. What type of relation is R?
options: Reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive
math1-w2-q3.explanation: a − a = 0 is divisible by 5 (reflexive). If a − b is divisible, then so is b − a = −(a − b) (symmetric). If a − b and b − c are both divisible, their sum a − c is also divisible (transitive). So it is an equivalence relation; skipping the transitive check is a common trap.

math1-w2-q4.question: Relation R on ℝ: a R b if a ≤ b. Which of these properties fails for R?
math1-w2-q4.explanation: a ≤ a is always true (reflexive), and a ≤ b and b ≤ c give a ≤ c (transitive). But 2 ≤ 5 holds while 5 ≤ 2 does not — so symmetry fails.

math1-w2-q5.question: f: ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = x². What is the range of this function?
math1-w2-q5.explanation: The square of an integer is always a perfect square: 0, 1, 4, 9, ... 'All non-negative integers' is the trap, because 2 or 3 never appear as outputs. The codomain is ℤ, but the range is smaller than it.

math1-w2-q6.question: How many different relations can be defined on a set A with 3 elements?
math1-w2-q6.explanation: A relation on A = a subset of A × A. |A × A| = 3 · 3 = 9, so subsets = 2⁹ = 512. 9 is just the count of pairs, not of relations; 64 = 2⁶ comes from mistakenly taking 3 + 3 = 6 pairs.

math1-w2-q7.question: If the ordered pairs (x + 1, 4) and (3, y − 2) are equal, what are x and y?
math1-w2-q7.explanation: Two ordered pairs are equal only when the first components are equal and the second ones are too: x + 1 = 3 gives x = 2, and y − 2 = 4 gives y = 6. y = 2 comes from not changing the sign when moving −2 to the other side. x = 3, y = 4 just copies the components across.

math1-w2-q8.question: f: {1, 2, 3, 4} → {1, 2, ..., 10}, f(x) = 2x + 1. What is the range of this function?
math1-w2-q8.explanation: Range = the outputs that actually occur: f(1) = 3, f(2) = 5, f(3) = 7, f(4) = 9, so the range is {3, 5, 7, 9}. {1, 2, ..., 10} is the codomain, not the range, and {1, 2, 3, 4} is the domain. {2, 4, 6, 8} forgets the + 1.

math1-w2-q9.question: R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (1, 3), (3, 1)} is a relation on A = {1, 2, 3}. Which pair must be added to make R reflexive?
math1-w2-q9.explanation: Reflexive needs (a, a) for every a in A: (1, 1) and (2, 2) are there, but (3, 3) is missing. The other pairs (2, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3) are not needed for reflexivity — reflexive only talks about the diagonal pairs (a, a).

math1-w2-q10.question: A = {p, q} and B = {1, 2, 3}. How many different functions from A to B are there?
math1-w2-q10.explanation: A function needs exactly one image for each element of A. p has 3 choices and q also has 3 choices, so 3 · 3 = 3² = 9 functions. 8 = 2³ comes from swapping the base and the power. 64 = 2⁶ counts all relations from A to B, not functions, and 6 = |A × B| is just the number of pairs.

math1-w2-q11.question: On the set {1, 2, ..., 10}, the relation R is: a R b if (a − b) is divisible by 4. What is the equivalence class of 2?
math1-w2-q11.explanation: The class of 2 contains every b for which 2 − b is divisible by 4, i.e. b leaves remainder 2 when divided by 4: 2, 6, 10. {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} is all the even numbers — 4 − 2 = 2 is not divisible by 4. {6, 10} leaves out 2 itself, although 2 R 2 is always true because R is reflexive.

math1-w2-q12.question: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2)}. What is true about R?
math1-w2-q12.explanation: All the (a, a) are present, so it is reflexive. (1, 2) comes with (2, 1) and (2, 3) with (3, 2), so it is symmetric. But (1, 2) and (2, 3) are both in R while (1, 3) is not — transitivity fails. So it is not an equivalence relation. Checking only the first two properties and calling it 'equivalence' is the main trap.

math1-w2-q13.question: How many relations on the set {a, b, c} are both reflexive and symmetric?
math1-w2-q13.explanation: Reflexive needs all three of (a, a), (b, b), (c, c) — there is no choice there. Symmetric makes the off-diagonal pairs come in couples: {(a, b), (b, a)}, {(a, c), (c, a)}, {(b, c), (c, b)} — each couple is either fully in or fully out. 3 couples with 2 choices each: 2³ = 8. 64 = 2⁶ counts the reflexive relations only (symmetry ignored), and 512 = 2⁹ counts all relations.

math1-w2-q14.question: A × B has exactly 6 elements, and (1, x), (2, y), (3, x) are among them (x ≠ y). Which of these pairs must be in A × B?
math1-w2-q14.explanation: From the given pairs, A has at least 1, 2, 3 and B has at least x, y. Then |A × B| ≥ 3 · 2 = 6, and it is exactly 6, so A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {x, y} exactly. Hence (2, x) must be there. (x, 2) and (y, 1) have the order reversed — the first component comes from A. 4 cannot be in A, otherwise there would be 8 elements.

math1-w2-q15.question: On ℤ, the relation R is: a R b if a + b is even. What is true about R?
options: It is an equivalence relation with 2 equivalence classes
It is reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive
It is symmetric, but not reflexive
It is an equivalence relation with infinitely many classes
math1-w2-q15.explanation: a + a = 2a is always even, so it is reflexive. a + b = b + a, so it is symmetric. If a + b and b + c are even, then a + c = (a + b) + (b + c) − 2b is even too — transitive. a + b is even exactly when a and b are both even or both odd, so there are only 2 classes: the even integers and the odd integers. Thinking 'a + a can be odd' is wrong, and assuming transitivity fails without checking is a trap too.

math1-w3-q1.question: What is the distance between the points (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
math1-w3-q1.explanation: √((4 − 1)² + (6 − 2)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. 25 comes from forgetting to take the square root; 7 = 3 + 4 comes from simply adding them, which is wrong.

math1-w3-q2.question: What is the slope of the line 3x + 4y − 12 = 0?
math1-w3-q2.explanation: 4y = −3x + 12, so y = −(3/4)x + 3, slope = −3/4. The formula −a/b also gives −3/4. Forgetting the minus sign gives 3/4, and flipping a/b gives −4/3.

math1-w3-q3.question: Which line is perpendicular to y = 2x + 5 and passes through the point (0, 1)?
math1-w3-q3.explanation: The given slope is 2, so the perpendicular slope = −1/2. It passes through (0, 1), so the y-intercept is 1: y = −x/2 + 1. y = 2x + 1 is a parallel line; y = x/2 + 1 forgets to change the sign.

math1-w3-q4.question: Which point divides the segment joining A(1, 2) and B(7, 8) internally in the ratio 1:2, measured from A?
math1-w3-q4.explanation: m:n = 1:2, point = ((1·7 + 2·1)/3, (1·8 + 2·2)/3) = (9/3, 12/3) = (3, 4). It should be close to A because its distance from A is smaller. (5, 6) comes from applying the ratio the other way round, and (4, 5) is the midpoint.

math1-w3-q5.question: The lines 2x + ky = 5 and 4x + 6y = 7 are parallel. What is the value of k?
math1-w3-q5.explanation: Slopes: −2/k and −4/6 = −2/3. For parallel lines −2/k = −2/3, so k = 3. Check: multiply 2x + 3y = 5 by 2 to get 4x + 6y = 10 — same direction, different line. −3 comes from a sign mistake.

math1-w3-q6.question: What is the perpendicular distance from the point (3, −2) to the line 4x − 3y + 2 = 0?
math1-w3-q6.explanation: |4·3 − 3·(−2) + 2| / √(4² + 3²) = |12 + 6 + 2| / 5 = 20/5 = 4. −3 · (−2) = +6; getting the sign wrong here gives 8/5. Forgetting the denominator √(a² + b²) gives 20.

math1-w3-q7.question: What is the midpoint of the points (−3, 5) and (7, −1)?
math1-w3-q7.explanation: Midpoint = ((−3 + 7)/2, (5 + (−1))/2) = (4/2, 4/2) = (2, 2). (4, 4) adds the coordinates but forgets to divide by 2. (10, −6) is the difference of the coordinates, and (5, −3) is half of that difference — the midpoint adds, it does not subtract.

math1-w3-q8.question: What is the slope of the line through the points (2, −1) and (5, 8)?
math1-w3-q8.explanation: Slope = (8 − (−1))/(5 − 2) = 9/3 = 3. 7/3 comes from writing −(−1) as −1. 1/3 puts the x and y differences the wrong way round, and −3 comes from taking one point first in the numerator and the other point first in the denominator.

math1-w3-q9.question: What is the y-intercept of the line 2x − 5y + 10 = 0?
math1-w3-q9.explanation: For the y-intercept put x = 0: −5y + 10 = 0, so y = 2. −5 is the x-intercept (putting y = 0 gives 2x + 10 = 0, x = −5). −2 is a sign mistake, and 10 is just the constant term, not the intercept.

math1-w3-q10.question: The points (1, 2), (3, 6) and (k, 10) lie on one line (collinear). What is the value of k?
math1-w3-q10.explanation: The slope of the first two points = (6 − 2)/(3 − 1) = 2. The third point is on the same line, so (10 − 2)/(k − 1) = 2, i.e. k − 1 = 4 and k = 5. 4 comes from taking k − 1 = 4 as the answer. 17 comes from inverting the slope (Δx/Δy), and −3 from reversing the order in the denominator to (1 − k).

math1-w3-q11.question: The lines 3x − 2y + 4 = 0 and kx + 6y − 1 = 0 are perpendicular to each other. What is the value of k?
math1-w3-q11.explanation: Slopes from −a/b: the first line has 3/2, the second −k/6. For perpendicular lines (3/2)(−k/6) = −1, i.e. −k/4 = −1 and k = 4. −9 comes from the parallel condition (−k/6 = 3/2). −4 comes from taking the first slope as −3/2 (a sign error in −a/b).

math1-w3-q12.question: Which line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining A(1, 3) and B(5, 7)?
math1-w3-q12.explanation: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to AB. Midpoint = (3, 5), slope of AB = (7 − 3)/(5 − 1) = 1, so the perpendicular slope = −1. y − 5 = −(x − 3) ⇒ x + y = 8. y = x + 2 is the line AB itself. x + y = 4 and x + y = 12 have the right slope but pass through A or B, not the midpoint.

math1-w3-q13.question: What is the distance between the parallel lines 3x + 4y − 7 = 0 and 6x + 8y + 6 = 0?
math1-w3-q13.explanation: Take a point on the first line: (1, 1), since 3 + 4 − 7 = 0. Its distance from the second line = |6·1 + 8·1 + 6| / √(6² + 8²) = 20/10 = 2. Or divide the second line by 2 (3x + 4y + 3 = 0), then |−7 − 3|/5 = 2. 13/5 comes from using |−7 − 6|/5 without first making the coefficients the same; 4/5 has a sign error, and 10 forgets to divide by √(a² + b²).

math1-w3-q14.question: The point P(4, y) lies on the segment joining A(2, −3) and B(8, 6). In what ratio does P divide the segment, counted from A, and what is y?
math1-w3-q14.explanation: Let the ratio be m:n. x-coordinate: (8m + 2n)/(m + n) = 4 ⇒ 8m + 2n = 4m + 4n ⇒ 4m = 2n ⇒ m:n = 1:2. Now y = (1·6 + 2·(−3))/3 = 0. 2:1 comes from swapping m and n in the section formula. 1:1 assumes the midpoint, but the midpoint has x-coordinate 5, not 4. '1:2 and y = 3' has the right ratio but uses the weights the wrong way round when finding y.

math1-w3-q15.question: What is the mirror image (reflection) of the point (3, 4) in the line x + y = 1?
math1-w3-q15.explanation: Go from (3, 4) perpendicular to the line: the line has slope −1, so the perpendicular slope is 1: y = x + 1. Solve it with x + y = 1: x = 0, y = 1, so the foot is (0, 1). The foot is the midpoint of the image and (3, 4), so image = (2·0 − 3, 2·1 − 4) = (−3, −2). Check: the midpoint (0, 1) is on the line ✓. (0, 1) is only the foot, not the image. (−4, −3) is the reflection in the line x + y = 0 (the 1 was forgotten), and (−2, −3) has the coordinates swapped.

math1-w4-q1.question: What is the x-coordinate of the vertex of f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 3?
math1-w4-q1.explanation: x = −b/(2a) = −(−8)/(2·2) = 8/4 = 2. Dropping the minus sign gives −2, and dividing by just a instead of 2a gives 4.

math1-w4-q2.question: What is true about the roots of the equation x² + 4x + 7 = 0?
options: One positive and one negative root
math1-w4-q2.explanation: D = 4² − 4·1·7 = 16 − 28 = −12 < 0, so there are no real roots; the parabola lies entirely above the x-axis. Saying 'two roots' just because b² is positive is wrong — you also have to subtract 4ac.

math1-w4-q3.question: What is the maximum value of f(x) = −x² + 4x + 1?
math1-w4-q3.explanation: a = −1 < 0, so the maximum is at the vertex. x = −4/(2·(−1)) = 2, f(2) = −4 + 8 + 1 = 5. 2 is only the x-coordinate of the vertex, not the value. −11 comes from substituting x = −2.

math1-w4-q4.question: If α, β are the roots of the equation 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0, what are α + β and αβ?
math1-w4-q4.explanation: α + β = −b/a = 5/2, αβ = c/a = 3/2. Check: the roots are 1 and 3/2, sum 5/2 and product 3/2 ✓. Forgetting the minus in the sum gives −5/2, and not dividing by a = 2 gives 5 and 3.

math1-w4-q5.question: The equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots and k > 0. What is k?
math1-w4-q5.explanation: For equal roots D = 0: k² − 36 = 0, so k = ±6; since k > 0, k = 6. 36 is k², not k. The equation then becomes (x + 3)² = 0.

math1-w4-q6.question: A parabola has vertex (1, −2) and passes through the point (3, 6). What is its equation?
math1-w4-q6.explanation: Vertex form: f(x) = a(x − 1)² − 2. Substitute (3, 6): 4a − 2 = 6, so a = 2. f(x) = 2(x − 1)² − 2 = 2x² − 4x. Option A assumes a = 1 (a was never found). 2x² + 4x uses (x + 1), i.e. the wrong sign for the vertex.

math1-w4-q7.question: What does the graph of f(x) = −2x² + 3x + 5 look like?
options: It opens upward and has a minimum at the vertex
It opens downward and has a maximum at the vertex
It opens upward and has a maximum at the vertex
It opens downward and has no maximum value
math1-w4-q7.explanation: The shape is decided only by a, the coefficient of x². Here a = −2 < 0, so the parabola opens downward and the vertex is the highest point — the maximum is there. Saying 'opens upward' because of +3x and +5 is wrong. A downward parabola always has a maximum value: at the vertex.

math1-w4-q8.question: What are the roots of the equation x² − 5x − 14 = 0?
math1-w4-q8.explanation: We need two numbers with product −14 and sum −5: −7 and 2. So x² − 5x − 14 = (x − 7)(x + 2), and the roots are x = 7, x = −2. Check: 49 − 35 − 14 = 0 ✓. '−7, 2' writes the numbers inside the factors as the roots — the roots have the opposite sign. 7 and 2 have product 14, not −14.

math1-w4-q9.question: What is true about the roots of the equation 4x² − 12x + 9 = 0?
math1-w4-q9.explanation: D = (−12)² − 4·4·9 = 144 − 144 = 0, so there is one repeated root: x = −b/(2a) = 12/8 = 3/2. This is (2x − 3)² = 0. x = 3 comes from dividing by a instead of 2a. D = 0 does not mean 'no root' — the graph touches the x-axis.

math1-w4-q10.question: Write f(x) = x² + 6x + 11 in vertex form by completing the square. What is the vertex?
math1-w4-q10.explanation: x² + 6x = (x + 3)² − 9, so f(x) = (x + 3)² − 9 + 11 = (x + 3)² + 2. From the vertex form a(x − h)² + k, h = −3 and k = 2: vertex (−3, 2). (3, 2) reads (x + 3) as x − 3. (−3, 11) forgets to adjust for the −9, and (−6, 11) uses −b/a instead of −b/(2a).

math1-w4-q11.question: One root of the equation x² + px − 12 = 0 is 3. What is the other root?
math1-w4-q11.explanation: Product of roots = c/a = −12, so 3 · β = −12 and β = −4. Or put x = 3: 9 + 3p − 12 = 0, p = 1; sum = −p = −1 = 3 + β, again β = −4. 4 comes from taking the product as +12. 1 is the value of p, and −1 is the sum of the roots, not the other root.

math1-w4-q12.question: For which values of k does the equation x² − 2kx + 9 = 0 have no real root?
math1-w4-q12.explanation: No real root needs D < 0: (−2k)² − 4·1·9 = 4k² − 36 < 0 ⇒ k² < 9 ⇒ −3 < k < 3. 'k < −3 or k > 3' is the condition for D > 0 (two distinct roots). 'k > 3' only thinks of the positive square root. −6 < k < 6 comes from taking b as k instead of −2k.

math1-w4-q13.question: If α, β are the roots of the equation x² − 4x + 1 = 0, what is α² + β²?
math1-w4-q13.explanation: α + β = −b/a = 4 and αβ = c/a = 1. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 16 − 2 = 14. 16 comes from treating α² + β² as (α + β)²; 18 uses +2αβ instead of −2αβ. You can also check with the roots 2 ± √3: (7 + 4√3) + (7 − 4√3) = 14 ✓.

math1-w4-q14.question: A farmer has 60 m of fencing. He makes a rectangular field along a straight wall, so fencing is needed on only three sides (the wall is the fourth side). What is the maximum possible area of the field (in m²)?
math1-w4-q14.explanation: Let the two sides perpendicular to the wall be x; the side parallel to the wall = 60 − 2x. Area A(x) = x(60 − 2x) = −2x² + 60x, a quadratic with a < 0. Vertex x = −60/(2·(−2)) = 15, so A = 15 · 30 = 450. 225 comes from taking a 15 × 15 square (fencing on all four sides). 900 comes from using x(60 − x), and 15 is just x, not the area.

math1-w4-q15.question: A quadratic function has roots 2 and −3, and its graph passes through the point (0, 12). What is the y-coordinate of its vertex?
math1-w4-q15.explanation: f(x) = a(x − 2)(x + 3). f(0) = a(−2)(3) = −6a = 12, so a = −2. The vertex lies midway between the roots: x = (2 + (−3))/2 = −1/2. f(−1/2) = −2(−5/2)(5/2) = 25/2. −25/2 comes from taking a = 2 (a sign error). 12 is the y-intercept, and −1/2 is the x-coordinate of the vertex.

math1-w5-q1.question: Which of these is NOT a polynomial?
math1-w5-q1.explanation: 2/x = 2x⁻¹, which has a negative power, so x² + 2/x is not a polynomial. The constant 5 is a polynomial of degree 0, and in √3·x² only the coefficient is irrational — the power is still 2, which is allowed.

math1-w5-q2.question: What is the degree of (x³ + 2x)(4x² − 1)?
math1-w5-q2.explanation: The product of the leading terms is x³ · 4x² = 4x⁵, so the degree is 3 + 2 = 5. 6 comes from multiplying the degrees.

math1-w5-q3.question: What is the remainder when p(x) = 2x³ − 3x² + x − 5 is divided by (x + 1)?
math1-w5-q3.explanation: For (x + 1), substitute x = −1: 2(−1) − 3(1) + (−1) − 5 = −2 − 3 − 1 − 5 = −11. −5 is p(1), which is what you would get when dividing by (x − 1).

math1-w5-q4.question: If (x − 2) is a factor of x³ − kx + 6, what is k?
math1-w5-q4.explanation: Factor theorem: p(2) = 0. 8 − 2k + 6 = 0, so 2k = 14, k = 7. Mistakenly substituting x = −2 gives −8 + 2k + 6 = 0, k = 1 — that is the trap.

math1-w5-q5.question: Simplify (x² + 3x − 1) − (2x² − x + 4).
math1-w5-q5.explanation: Change every sign in the second bracket: x² + 3x − 1 − 2x² + x − 4 = −x² + 4x − 5. Applying the minus only to the first term gives −x² + 2x + 3 — this is the most common mistake.

math1-w5-q6.question: p(x) = (x + 1)²(x − 2)(x − 3). For which of the given x values is p(x) < 0?
math1-w5-q6.explanation: (x + 1)² is never negative, so the sign is decided by (x − 2)(x − 3), which is negative only for 2 < x < 3. x = 2.5: (3.5)²(0.5)(−0.5) < 0 ✓. At x = −2, p = 1·(−4)(−5) = 20 > 0 — −1 is a root of even multiplicity, so the sign does not change there.

math1-w5-q7.question: What are the degree and the leading coefficient of the polynomial 7 − 3x² + 5x⁴ − x?
math1-w5-q7.explanation: The highest power is x⁴, so the degree is 4, and its coefficient 5 is the leading coefficient. 7 is just the term written first (the constant) — the leading coefficient is decided by the highest power, not by the order of writing. 'Degree 5, leading coefficient 4' swaps the power and the coefficient.

math1-w5-q8.question: What is the remainder when p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 4 is divided by (x − 3)?
math1-w5-q8.explanation: Remainder theorem: for (x − 3) find p(3): 27 − 18 + 4 = 13. −41 = p(−3), which is the remainder for (x + 3). 49 comes from taking −2x² as +18, and 4 is just the constant term.

math1-w5-q9.question: At most how many turning points can the graph of a degree 5 polynomial have?
math1-w5-q9.explanation: A degree n polynomial has at most n − 1 turning points, so 5 − 1 = 4. 5 is the maximum number of real roots, not of turning points. 'At most' means there can be fewer (x⁵ has no turning point at all), but never more than 4.

math1-w5-q10.question: When (2x² − x + 3)(x² + 4x − 1) is expanded, what is the coefficient of x²?
math1-w5-q10.explanation: x² arises in three ways: 2x² · (−1) = −2x², (−x) · 4x = −4x², and 3 · x² = 3x². Total −2 − 4 + 3 = −3. 5 comes from taking (−x)(4x) as +4x². −6 misses the 3 · x² term — check every pair whose powers add up to 2.

math1-w5-q11.question: What is the quotient when 2x³ − 3x² + 4x − 1 is divided by (x − 1)?
math1-w5-q11.explanation: Synthetic division with 1: coefficients 2, −3, 4, −1 → 2; 2·1 − 3 = −1; −1·1 + 4 = 3; 3·1 − 1 = 2. Quotient 2x² − x + 3, remainder 2. Check: (x − 1)(2x² − x + 3) + 2 = 2x³ − 3x² + 4x − 1 ✓. 2x² − 5x + 9 comes from dividing with −1 instead of 1, i.e. it is the quotient for (x + 1).

math1-w5-q12.question: p(x) = x³ + ax² + bx − 6. (x − 1) is a factor of p(x), and dividing p(x) by (x + 1) leaves remainder 4. What are a and b?
math1-w5-q12.explanation: Factor theorem: p(1) = 1 + a + b − 6 = 0 ⇒ a + b = 5. Remainder theorem: p(−1) = −1 + a − b − 6 = 4 ⇒ a − b = 11. Adding, 2a = 16, a = 8, b = −3. 'a = 6, b = −1' comes from using p(−1) = 0 (ignoring the remainder 4). 'a = 8, b = 1' applies the two conditions the wrong way round, and 'a = −3, b = 8' swaps a and b.

math1-w5-q13.question: A cubic polynomial p(x) has roots 1, −2 and 3, and p(0) = 12. What is p(2)?
math1-w5-q13.explanation: By the factor theorem p(x) = a(x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3). p(0) = a(−1)(2)(−3) = 6a = 12, so a = 2. p(2) = 2(1)(4)(−1) = −8. −4 comes from assuming a = 1 (the p(0) condition was never used). 8 drops the sign of (2 − 3) = −1, and 12 is p(0).

math1-w5-q14.question: A polynomial p(x) leaves remainder 5 when divided by (x − 2), and remainder −1 when divided by (x + 1). What is the remainder when p(x) is divided by (x − 2)(x + 1)?
math1-w5-q14.explanation: The divisor has degree 2, so the remainder is r(x) = mx + c (degree < 2). p(x) = (x − 2)(x + 1)q(x) + mx + c. Put x = 2: 2m + c = 5; put x = −1: −m + c = −1. Subtracting, 3m = 6, m = 2, c = 1: remainder 2x + 1. x + 3 satisfies only the first condition (5 at x = 2) and gives 2 at x = −1. 4 = 5 + (−1) and −5 = 5 · (−1) add or multiply the remainders, which is not the right method.

math1-w5-q15.question: Which statement about p(x) = −(x + 1)²(x − 3) is true?
options: At x = −1 the graph crosses the x-axis
At x = 3 the graph only touches the x-axis
math1-w5-q15.explanation: The leading term is −x³ (degree 3, coefficient −1), so as x → ∞, p(x) → −∞ — this is true. −1 has multiplicity 2 (even), so the graph only touches there, it does not cross. 3 has multiplicity 1 (odd), so the graph crosses there. At x = −2, p = −(1)(−5) = 5 > 0, so p(x) is positive for x < −1, not negative.

math1-w6-q1.question: f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x². What kind of function is this?
math1-w6-q1.explanation: f(2) = f(−2) = 4, so it is not one-one. Negative numbers (like −1) never appear as outputs, so it is not onto the codomain ℝ either. Only with domain [0, ∞) and codomain [0, ∞) does it become bijective.

math1-w6-q2.question: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x². What is (g∘f)(1)?
math1-w6-q2.explanation: (g∘f)(1) = g(f(1)) = g(3) = 9. 3 comes from reversing the order and computing (f∘g)(1) = f(1) = 3.

math1-w6-q3.question: What is the inverse function of f(x) = (x − 5)/2?
math1-w6-q3.explanation: y = (x − 5)/2 ⇒ 2y = x − 5 ⇒ x = 2y + 5. Swapping gives f⁻¹(x) = 2x + 5. Check: f(f⁻¹(1)) = f(7) = 1 ✓. 2/(x − 5) is the reciprocal, not the inverse.

math1-w6-q4.question: Which of these functions f: ℝ → ℝ is bijective?
math1-w6-q4.explanation: x³ is strictly increasing (one-one) and every real number has a real cube root (onto). eˣ is one-one but never gives negative values or 0, so it is not onto ℝ — this is the most common trap. x² and |x| are not even one-one.

math1-w6-q5.question: How is the graph of y = (x − 3)² + 2 obtained by shifting the graph of y = x²?
math1-w6-q5.explanation: f(x − 3) moves the graph 3 units right (don't think 'left' just because you see a minus), and + 2 moves the graph 2 units up. The vertex moves from (0, 0) to (3, 2).

math1-w6-q6.question: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. What is (f∘g)⁻¹(7)?
math1-w6-q6.explanation: (f∘g)(x) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. (f∘g)⁻¹(7) means the x for which 2x + 1 = 7, i.e. x = 3. Another way: g⁻¹(f⁻¹(7)) = g⁻¹(2) = 3. Taking the order the other way round gives f⁻¹(g⁻¹(7)) = 5/2; 15 is (f∘g)(7).

math1-w6-q7.question: f(x) = 4x − 3. What is f⁻¹(5)?
math1-w6-q7.explanation: f⁻¹(5) is the input whose output is 5: 4x − 3 = 5 ⇒ x = 2. Check: f(2) = 5 ✓. 17 is f(5) — the inverse swaps input and output. 1/17 = 1/f(5) is a reciprocal; f⁻¹ does not mean 1/f.

math1-w6-q8.question: f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = 3x. What is (f∘g)(x)?
math1-w6-q8.explanation: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(3x) = 3x + 4 — first g, then f. 3x + 12 = g(f(x)) = 3(x + 4), i.e. the order reversed. 3x² + 12x is the product f(x) · g(x), not a composition.

math1-w6-q9.question: Which of these functions f: ℝ → ℝ is one-one?
math1-w6-q9.explanation: 5 − 2x is a straight line with slope −2; every horizontal line cuts it only once, so it is one-one. The other three fail: for x² + 1, f(1) = f(−1) = 2; for |x − 2|, f(0) = f(4) = 2; and for (x − 1)², f(0) = f(2) = 1. A decreasing function is one-one too — it does not have to be increasing.

math1-w6-q10.question: Transforming the graph of y = |x| gives y = −|x + 2| + 3. Where is the 'corner' point (vertex) of the new graph?
math1-w6-q10.explanation: |x + 2| = f(x − (−2)), so the graph moves 2 units left; the − sign reflects it in the x-axis (the V turns upside down), and + 3 moves it 3 units up. Vertex (0, 0) → (−2, 0) → (−2, 3). (2, 3) reads + 2 as a right shift. The reflection does not move the vertex because it is on y = 0, so the options with −3 are wrong.

math1-w6-q11.question: For f: ℝ → [k, ∞), f(x) = x² − 4x + 7 to be onto, what must k be?
math1-w6-q11.explanation: Onto means range = codomain. Find the range: a = 1 > 0, vertex x = −(−4)/2 = 2, minimum f(2) = 4 − 8 + 7 = 3. The range is [3, ∞), so k = 3. 2 is only the x-coordinate of the vertex, and 7 = f(0) is the y-intercept — not the minimum value.

math1-w6-q12.question: f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3), x ≠ 3. What is f⁻¹(x)?
math1-w6-q12.explanation: y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) ⇒ xy − 3y = 2x + 1 ⇒ x(y − 2) = 3y + 1 ⇒ x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2). Swapping gives f⁻¹(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 2). Check: f(0) = −1/3, and f⁻¹(−1/3) = 0/(−7/3) = 0 ✓. (x − 3)/(2x + 1) is the reciprocal 1/f(x), not the inverse. (2x − 1)/(x + 3) just flips every sign — that is not how the inverse of a rational function is found; you must solve for x.

math1-w6-q13.question: g(x) = 3x + 2 and f(g(x)) = 6x + 7. What is f(x)?
math1-w6-q13.explanation: Let u = g(x) = 3x + 2, so x = (u − 2)/3. f(u) = 6 · (u − 2)/3 + 7 = 2u − 4 + 7 = 2u + 3, i.e. f(x) = 2x + 3. Check: f(3x + 2) = 6x + 4 + 3 = 6x + 7 ✓. 3x + 5 = (6x + 7) − (3x + 2) just subtracts; 18x + 19 puts 3x + 2 into (6x + 7) — the order reversed. 2x + 7 forgets the −4 adjustment.

math1-w6-q14.question: f: [3, ∞) → [1, ∞), f(x) = x² − 6x + 10 is bijective. What is f⁻¹(10)?
math1-w6-q14.explanation: f⁻¹(10) is the x for which f(x) = 10: x² − 6x + 10 = 10 ⇒ x(x − 6) = 0 ⇒ x = 0 or 6. The domain is [3, ∞), so only x = 6 is valid. An inverse function has only one output, so 'both' is wrong — f became one-one precisely by restricting the domain. 50 = f(10), not f⁻¹(10).

math1-w6-q15.question: Shifting the graph of y = f(x) 2 units left and 3 units down gives the graph of y = x² + 4x + 1. What is f(x)?
math1-w6-q15.explanation: 2 left and 3 down means the new graph is f(x + 2) − 3. So f(x + 2) − 3 = x² + 4x + 1 = (x + 2)² − 3, i.e. f(x + 2) = (x + 2)², hence f(x) = x². Undoing it also works: move the new graph 2 right and 3 up: (x − 2 + 2)² − 3 + 3 = x² ✓. (x + 4)² comes from shifting left again when going back; x² − 6 has the vertical shift in the wrong direction, and x² + 4x + 4 never undoes the horizontal shift.

math1-w7-q1.question: What is the value of log₂(64)?
math1-w7-q1.explanation: 2⁶ = 64, so log₂(64) = 6. 8 comes from taking √64, and 32 from computing 64/2 — log means 'which power'.

math1-w7-q2.question: Which statement about f(x) = (1/2)ˣ is correct?
options: Its range is (0, ∞) and it is decreasing
Its range is all real numbers
math1-w7-q2.explanation: The base 1/2 < 1, so the function is decreasing, and aˣ is always positive, so the range is (0, ∞). The graph passes through (0, 1), not (1, 0) — (1, 0) is a point on the log graph.

math1-w7-q3.question: What is the value of log₁₀(50) + log₁₀(2)?
math1-w7-q3.explanation: Product rule: log(50) + log(2) = log(100) = 2, because 10² = 100. log(52) is the trap — when you add logs, the numbers get multiplied, not added. 100 is the value inside, not the log.

math1-w7-q4.question: Solve: 3^(2x − 1) = 27.
math1-w7-q4.explanation: 27 = 3³, so 2x − 1 = 3, 2x = 4, x = 2. Check: 3³ = 27 ✓. x = 14 comes from writing 2x − 1 = 27 (forgetting to make the bases the same); 3/2 comes from ignoring the −1.

math1-w7-q5.question: What is the value of log₄(8)?
math1-w7-q5.explanation: 4ʸ = 8 ⇒ 2^(2y) = 2³ ⇒ 2y = 3 ⇒ y = 3/2. Change of base also gives: log₂8 / log₂4 = 3/2. 2/3 comes from writing the fraction upside down, i.e. log₈(4).

math1-w7-q6.question: Solve: log₃(x) + log₃(x − 8) = 2.
math1-w7-q6.explanation: log₃(x(x − 8)) = 2 ⇒ x² − 8x = 9 ⇒ x² − 8x − 9 = 0 ⇒ (x − 9)(x + 1) = 0. At x = −1, log₃(−1) is not defined, so reject it. Only x = 9: log₃9 + log₃1 = 2 + 0 = 2 ✓. Keeping both roots is the main trap.

math1-w7-q7.question: What is the value of (3²)³ / 3⁴?
math1-w7-q7.explanation: (3²)³ = 3⁶ (the powers multiply), and 3⁶ / 3⁴ = 3⁶⁻⁴ = 3² = 9. 3 comes from taking (3²)³ as 3²⁺³ = 3⁵. 81 comes from reading (3²)³ as 3^(2³) = 3⁸, and 1/9 does the division the wrong way round.

math1-w7-q8.question: What is the value of log₅(1/125)?
math1-w7-q8.explanation: 1/125 = 1/5³ = 5⁻³, so log₅(1/125) = −3. 3 is log₅(125) — 1/125 means a negative power. 1/3 and −1/3 come from treating the log as 'divide by how much'; a log gives the power.

math1-w7-q9.question: What is the domain of f(x) = log₂(x − 4)?
math1-w7-q9.explanation: A log is defined only for positive numbers, so x − 4 > 0, i.e. x > 4. x ≥ 4 is wrong because x = 4 gives log₂(0), which is not defined. x > 0 comes from ignoring the − 4 inside.

math1-w7-q10.question: What is the value of log₂(3) · log₃(16)?
math1-w7-q10.explanation: Change of base: log₂(3) = ln 3/ln 2 and log₃(16) = ln 16/ln 3. The product = ln 16/ln 2 = log₂(16) = 4 — ln 3 cancels. log₂ 48 comes from treating a product of logs as the log of a product (3 · 16); that rule is only log(xy) = log x + log y. 16 is the number inside, not the log.

math1-w7-q11.question: A town has a population of 2000, growing by 10% every year (compound growth). What will the population be after 2 years?
math1-w7-q11.explanation: A = P(1 + r)ᵗ = 2000 · (1.1)² = 2000 · 1.21 = 2420. 2400 comes from adding 10% of the original 2000 (200) each year — that is simple growth, not exponential. 2200 is the population after just 1 year.

math1-w7-q12.question: The amount of a medicine in the body halves every 4 hours. How many hours will it take to go from 800 mg to 50 mg?
math1-w7-q12.explanation: Amount = 800 · (1/2)^(t/4). 800 · (1/2)^(t/4) = 50 ⇒ (1/2)^(t/4) = 1/16 = (1/2)⁴ ⇒ t/4 = 4 ⇒ t = 16 hours. By steps too: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50, i.e. 4 halvings × 4 hours. 4 is only the number of halvings, not hours; 12 counts one halving too few. 64 comes from treating 800/50 = 16 as the number of halvings and multiplying by 4.

math1-w7-q13.question: What are all the solutions of the equation 4ˣ − 6 · 2ˣ + 8 = 0?
math1-w7-q13.explanation: 4ˣ = (2ˣ)², so put u = 2ˣ: u² − 6u + 8 = 0 ⇒ (u − 2)(u − 4) = 0 ⇒ u = 2 or 4. 2ˣ = 2 ⇒ x = 1, and 2ˣ = 4 ⇒ x = 2. Both are valid because 2 and 4 are positive (2ˣ is always positive). 'x = 2 or x = 4' writes the values of u as x — you still have to solve 2ˣ = u.

math1-w7-q14.question: Solve: log₂(x) + log₄(x) = 6.
math1-w7-q14.explanation: Make the bases the same: log₄(x) = log₂(x)/log₂(4) = log₂(x)/2. So log₂x + (1/2)log₂x = 6 ⇒ (3/2)log₂x = 6 ⇒ log₂x = 4 ⇒ x = 16. Check: log₂16 + log₄16 = 4 + 2 = 6 ✓. x = 8 comes from treating log₄ as log₂ too (2 log₂x = 6). x = 4 comes from writing log₄x = 2 log₂x (the fraction upside down), and x = 64 drops the second term.

math1-w7-q15.question: If log₁₀2 = a and log₁₀3 = b, what is log₁₀(7.2)?
math1-w7-q15.explanation: 7.2 = 72/10 = (2³ · 3²)/10. So log(7.2) = 3 log 2 + 2 log 3 − log 10 = 3a + 2b − 1. '3a + 2b' is log 72 — it forgets the −1 from the /10. 2a + 3b − 1 has the powers swapped (72 = 2³ · 3², not 2² · 3³). 6ab − 1 turns the product inside the log into a product of logs, whereas log(xy) = log x + log y.

math1-w8-q2.question: What is lim(n→∞) 1/n?
math1-w8-q2.explanation: The bigger n gets, the closer 1/n gets to 0 (1/1000, 1/1000000, ...). It never becomes exactly 0, but the limit is still 0 — for a limit, 'getting arbitrarily close' is enough.

math1-w8-q3.question: What is lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2)?
math1-w8-q3.explanation: Substituting directly gives 0/0. x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2); cancel to get x + 2, which is 4 at x = 2. Saying 'the limit does not exist' just because you see 0/0 is wrong.

math1-w8-q4.question: What is the sum of the infinite GP 6 + 3 + 3/2 + 3/4 + ...?
math1-w8-q4.explanation: a = 6, r = 1/2 (|r| < 1). S∞ = 6/(1 − 1/2) = 6/(1/2) = 12. 10.5 is just the sum of the first three terms, and infinitely many terms do not mean an infinite sum when r is small.

math1-w8-q5.question: What is lim(x→∞) (3x² + 5)/(2x² − x)?
math1-w8-q5.explanation: Divide the top and bottom by x²: (3 + 5/x²)/(2 − 1/x). As x → ∞, 5/x² → 0 and 1/x → 0, so the limit = 3/2. The degrees are equal, so the answer is the ratio of the leading coefficients — not 0 or ∞.

math1-w8-q6.question: f(x) = x + 1 when x < 1, and f(x) = 3x − k when x ≥ 1. What must k be for f to be continuous at x = 1?
math1-w8-q6.explanation: Left-hand limit = 1 + 1 = 2. The right side and f(1) = 3 − k. For continuity 3 − k = 2, so k = 1. k = 2 comes from taking the LHL itself as k.

math1-w8-q7.question: What is the 6th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...?
math1-w8-q7.explanation: a = 3, r = 2: a₆ = a · r⁵ = 3 · 32 = 96. 192 = 3 · 2⁶ comes from using the power n instead of n − 1. 18 = 3 + 5 · 3 is the AP formula — in a GP each step multiplies, it does not add.

math1-w8-q8.question: What is the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 2, 5, 8, 11, ...?
math1-w8-q8.explanation: a = 2, d = 3, n = 20: S₂₀ = (20/2)[2·2 + 19·3] = 10 · 61 = 610. 640 comes from using nd = 60 instead of (n − 1)d. 1220 multiplies by n instead of n/2, and 59 is the 20th term, not the sum.

math1-w8-q9.question: Which of these sequences is convergent?
math1-w8-q9.explanation: (2n + 1)/n = 2 + 1/n, and 1/n → 0, so it converges to 2. (−1)ⁿ keeps jumping between −1 and 1 and never settles near one number — divergent. n² and 2ⁿ grow without bound, so they are divergent.

math1-w8-q10.question: What is lim(x→∞) (5x + 3)/(x² + 1)?
math1-w8-q10.explanation: Divide top and bottom by x²: (5/x + 3/x²)/(1 + 1/x²). As x → ∞ the numerator → 0 and the denominator → 1, so the limit is 0. The denominator has the higher degree (2), so it grows faster. 5 comes from taking the ratio of leading coefficients even though the degrees differ — that rule is only for equal degrees.

math1-w8-q11.question: What is lim(x→1) (x² + 2x − 3)/(x² − 1)?
math1-w8-q11.explanation: Direct substitution gives 0/0. Factorise: (x + 3)(x − 1) / ((x − 1)(x + 1)) = (x + 3)/(x + 1). Now put x = 1: 4/2 = 2. 4 comes from putting the value only into the numerator (x + 3) after cancelling. Saying 'does not exist' on seeing 0/0 is wrong — 0/0 means simplify further.

math1-w8-q12.question: The 4th term of an AP is 14 and the 9th term is 34. What is the sum of the first 15 terms of this AP?
math1-w8-q12.explanation: a + 3d = 14 and a + 8d = 34. Subtracting, 5d = 20, d = 4, and a = 2. S₁₅ = (15/2)[2·2 + 14·4] = 7.5 · 60 = 450. 480 comes from using 15d instead of 14d. 58 = a₁₅ is the 15th term, not the sum, and 900 uses n instead of n/2.

math1-w8-q13.question: An infinite GP has first term 8 and sum 24. What is the 3rd term of this GP?
math1-w8-q13.explanation: S∞ = a/(1 − r): 8/(1 − r) = 24 ⇒ 1 − r = 1/3 ⇒ r = 2/3 (|r| < 1 ✓). 3rd term = a · r² = 8 · 4/9 = 32/9. 16/3 = a · r is the second term. 2/3 is r itself, and 8/9 comes from mistaking 1 − r = 1/3 for r = 1/3.

math1-w8-q14.question: f(x) = (x² − 5x + 6)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, and f(2) = k. For f to be continuous at x = 2, what must k be?
math1-w8-q14.explanation: Continuity needs f(2) = lim(x→2) f(x). x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so for x ≠ 2, f(x) = x − 3, and the limit = 2 − 3 = −1. Hence k = −1. 0 comes from putting x = 2 into the numerator only. The 0/0 does not make continuity impossible — the limit exists, and f(2) just has to equal it.

math1-w8-q15.question: What is the sum of the infinite GP 9 − 6 + 4 − 8/3 + ...?
math1-w8-q15.explanation: r = −6/9 = −2/3, and |r| < 1, so the sum is finite: S∞ = 9/(1 − (−2/3)) = 9/(5/3) = 27/5. 27 comes from dropping the minus sign of r and using 9/(1 − 2/3). 13/3 is just the sum of the first 4 terms. Alternating signs do not make the sum infinite — only |r| < 1 matters.

math1-w9-q1.question: What is the derivative of 4x³ − 2x + 7?
math1-w9-q1.explanation: d/dx(4x³) = 12x², d/dx(−2x) = −2, d/dx(7) = 0. Total 12x² − 2. Adding the constant 7 to −2 (12x² + 5) is wrong, because the derivative of a constant is 0.

math1-w9-q2.question: What is the slope of the tangent to the curve y = x² at the point where x = 3?
math1-w9-q2.explanation: Slope = f′(3), and f′(x) = 2x, so f′(3) = 6. 9 is f(3), the y-coordinate of the point, not the slope.

math1-w9-q3.question: What is d/dx (x² · eˣ)?
math1-w9-q3.explanation: Product rule: (x²)′·eˣ + x²·(eˣ)′ = 2x·eˣ + x²·eˣ = eˣ(x² + 2x). 2x·eˣ is only one part — it comes from mistakenly doing something like (uv)′ = u′v′.

math1-w9-q4.question: What is d/dx (3x + 1)⁵?
math1-w9-q4.explanation: Chain rule: 5(3x + 1)⁴ · d/dx(3x + 1) = 5(3x + 1)⁴ · 3 = 15(3x + 1)⁴. 5(3x + 1)⁴ forgets the inner derivative 3; 15(3x + 1)⁵ forgets to reduce the power.

math1-w9-q5.question: What is the equation of the tangent line to the curve y = x² + 1 at the point where x = 1?
math1-w9-q5.explanation: Point: f(1) = 2, so (1, 2). Slope: f′(x) = 2x, f′(1) = 2. Tangent: y − 2 = 2(x − 1) ⇒ y = 2x. Check: at x = 1, y = 2 ✓. y = 2x + 2 does not even pass through the point (1, 2).

math1-w9-q6.question: What is the local minimum value of f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 1?
math1-w9-q6.explanation: f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), critical points x = 1, 2. f″(x) = 12x − 18: f″(1) = −6 (max), f″(2) = 6 (min). f(2) = 16 − 36 + 24 + 1 = 5. 6 = f(1) is the local maximum value, and 2 is only the x-coordinate of the min.

math1-w9-q7.question: What is the derivative of 5/x²?
math1-w9-q7.explanation: 5/x² = 5x⁻². Power rule: 5 · (−2) · x⁻³ = −10x⁻³ = −10/x³. 10/x³ drops the minus sign of the negative power. −10/x lowers the power by two; the power rule lowers it by just 1 (−2 → −3).

math1-w9-q8.question: f(x) = 3eˣ + ln x. What is f′(1)?
math1-w9-q8.explanation: f′(x) = 3eˣ + 1/x, so f′(1) = 3e + 1. 3e comes from forgetting the derivative of ln x (or seeing ln 1 = 0 and taking it as 0 — but the derivative is 1/x, which is 1 at x = 1). e + 1 drops the constant 3.

math1-w9-q9.question: On which interval is f(x) = x² − 6x increasing?
math1-w9-q9.explanation: f′(x) = 2x − 6. Increasing needs f′(x) > 0: 2x − 6 > 0 ⇒ x > 3. For x < 3, f′ < 0, so it is decreasing there. x > 6 comes from looking at the roots 0 and 6 — increasing/decreasing is decided by the sign of f′, not by the roots of f.

math1-w9-q10.question: What is d/dx [x/(x + 1)]?
math1-w9-q10.explanation: Quotient rule: (u′v − uv′)/v² = (1 · (x + 1) − x · 1)/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)². −1/(x + 1)² comes from reversing the order in the numerator (uv′ − u′v). 1 = u′/v′, which is not the quotient rule. (2x + 1)/(x + 1)² uses a plus instead of the minus.

math1-w9-q11.question: f(x) = e^(x²). What is f′(1)?
math1-w9-q11.explanation: Chain rule: f′(x) = e^(x²) · d/dx(x²) = 2x · e^(x²). At x = 1 this is 2 · e¹ = 2e. e comes from forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inner x² (2x) — the derivative of eˣ is eˣ, but that of e^(x²) is not just e^(x²).

math1-w9-q12.question: At which point on the curve y = x² − 4x + 1 is the tangent parallel to the line y = 2x + 5?
math1-w9-q12.explanation: Parallel means the tangent has slope 2: y′ = 2x − 4 = 2 ⇒ x = 3. y = 9 − 12 + 1 = −2, so the point is (3, −2). (1, −2) is also on the curve, but the slope there is 2·1 − 4 = −2 — the sign of the slope was taken wrongly. (2, −3) is the vertex, where the slope is 0, and (3, 2) has a sign error in finding y.

math1-w9-q13.question: An open box is made from a 12 cm × 12 cm square sheet by cutting squares of side x cm from all four corners and folding up the sides. What is the maximum possible volume of the box (in cm³)?
math1-w9-q13.explanation: Base (12 − 2x) × (12 − 2x), height x: V(x) = x(12 − 2x)², 0 < x < 6. V′(x) = (12 − 2x)² − 4x(12 − 2x) = (12 − 2x)(12 − 6x) = 0 ⇒ x = 2 (x = 6 gives V = 0). V(2) = 2 · 8² = 128. Check with the second derivative or with values: V(1) = 100, V(3) = 108, both smaller. 2 is just x, not the volume; 64 is the base area, forgetting to multiply by the height. 108 = V(3) comes from guessing x = 3 without using the derivative.

math1-w9-q14.question: A tangent line is drawn to the curve y = x³ − 2x at the point where x = 2. Where does this tangent cut the y-axis (its y-intercept)?
math1-w9-q14.explanation: Point: f(2) = 8 − 4 = 4, so (2, 4). Slope: f′(x) = 3x² − 2, f′(2) = 10. Tangent: y − 4 = 10(x − 2) ⇒ y = 10x − 16, so the y-intercept is −16. −20 comes from taking f′(x) = 3x² (forgetting the derivative of −2x): y = 12x − 20. 4 is the y-coordinate of the point, and 16 is a sign error.

math1-w9-q15.question: What do you get when you simplify d/dx [x · (2x − 1)³]?
math1-w9-q15.explanation: Product rule + chain rule: 1 · (2x − 1)³ + x · 3(2x − 1)² · 2 = (2x − 1)²[(2x − 1) + 6x] = (2x − 1)²(8x − 1). (2x − 1)²(5x − 1) comes from forgetting the inner derivative 2 in the chain rule (3x instead of 6x). 6x(2x − 1)² is only uv′ — the u′v part of the product rule is missing.

math1-w10-q1.question: What is ∫(6x² + 2) dx?
math1-w10-q1.explanation: ∫6x² dx = 6·x³/3 = 2x³, ∫2 dx = 2x. Total 2x³ + 2x + C. 12x is the derivative, not the integral. 6x³ forgets to divide by 3.

math1-w10-q2.question: What is the value of ∫₀³ 2x dx?
math1-w10-q2.explanation: The antiderivative is x², so 3² − 0² = 9. Geometrically too: a triangle with base 3 and height 6, area = (1/2)·3·6 = 9. 6 = f(3), not the integral; 18 comes from forgetting the 1/2.

math1-w10-q3.question: What is the value of ∫₁ᵉ (1/x) dx?
math1-w10-q3.explanation: ∫(1/x) dx = ln x. ln(e) − ln(1) = 1 − 0 = 1. e − 1 comes from mistakenly taking ∫(1/x) dx = x.

math1-w10-q4.question: What is the area between the curves y = x and y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1?
math1-w10-q4.explanation: For 0 < x < 1, x ≥ x², so upper = x, lower = x². Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. 5/6 comes from adding the two areas instead of subtracting.

math1-w10-q5.question: What is ∫ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx?
math1-w10-q5.explanation: u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx. Integral = ∫u³ du = u⁴/4 + C = (x² + 1)⁴/4 + C. Check: derivative = 4(x² + 1)³·2x/4 = 2x(x² + 1)³ ✓. Keeping 2x outside is wrong — it has been absorbed into du.

math1-w10-q6.question: What is the value of ∫₋₁² (x² − 2x) dx?
math1-w10-q6.explanation: F(x) = x³/3 − x². F(2) = 8/3 − 4 = −4/3, F(−1) = −1/3 − 1 = −4/3. F(2) − F(−1) = 0. The function is positive from −1 to 0 (area 4/3) and negative from 0 to 2 (area 4/3), and the two cancel. 8/3 is the total geometric area, not the definite integral.

math1-w10-q7.question: What is ∫(1/x + eˣ) dx?
math1-w10-q7.explanation: ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| and ∫eˣ dx = eˣ, so the answer is ln|x| + eˣ + C. −1/x² is the derivative of 1/x, not its integral. eˣ⁺¹/(x + 1) applies the power rule to eˣ — the power rule is only for xⁿ, and 1/x (n = −1) is its exception.

math1-w10-q8.question: What is the value of ∫₁² 3x² dx?
math1-w10-q8.explanation: The antiderivative is x³ (3 · x³/3). F(2) − F(1) = 8 − 1 = 7. 8 comes from forgetting to subtract F(1) at the lower limit. 21 = 24 − 3 comes from writing the integral of 3x² as 3x³ (no division by 3). 12 = 3 · 2² is a value of the function, not the integral.

math1-w10-q9.question: F′(x) = 4x and F(0) = 3. What is F(2)?
math1-w10-q9.explanation: F(x) = ∫4x dx = 2x² + C. F(0) = C = 3, so F(x) = 2x² + 3 and F(2) = 8 + 3 = 11. 8 comes from dropping the + C (that is, the 3). 19 = 4 · 4 + 3 forgets to divide by 2 after raising the power.

math1-w10-q10.question: What is the total area (geometric area, every part counted positive) between the line y = x − 1 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 3?
math1-w10-q10.explanation: The line crosses the x-axis at x = 1. From 0 to 1 it is below: area 1/2 (triangle, base 1, height 1). From 1 to 3 it is above: area 2 (base 2, height 2). Total area = 1/2 + 2 = 5/2. 3/2 = ∫₀³ (x − 1) dx is the net signed area, where the part below counts as minus. 2 takes only the part above.

math1-w10-q11.question: What is ∫ 3x² · e^(x³) dx?
math1-w10-q11.explanation: Put u = x³, du = 3x² dx. The integral = ∫eᵘ du = eᵘ + C = e^(x³) + C. Check: d/dx e^(x³) = e^(x³) · 3x² ✓. 3e^(x³) counts the 3 twice — it is already absorbed into du. e^(x³)/(3x²) divides by the inner derivative, which is not how substitution works.

math1-w10-q12.question: What is the area of the region enclosed between the curves y = 4 − x² and y = x + 2?
math1-w10-q12.explanation: Intersection: 4 − x² = x + 2 ⇒ x² + x − 2 = 0 ⇒ x = −2, 1. In between, the parabola is on top (at x = 0, 4 > 2). Area = ∫₋₂¹ [(4 − x²) − (x + 2)] dx = ∫₋₂¹ (2 − x − x²) dx = [2x − x²/2 − x³/3] from −2 to 1 = 7/6 − (−10/3) = 9/2. −9/2 comes from using lower − upper instead of upper − lower (an area cannot be negative). 7/6 takes only the value at the upper limit, and 27/2 adds the two curves instead of subtracting.

math1-w10-q13.question: What is the value of ∫₀² x/(x² + 1) dx?
math1-w10-q13.explanation: u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2. Limits: x = 0 ⇒ u = 1, x = 2 ⇒ u = 5. Integral = (1/2)∫₁⁵ (1/u) du = (1/2)(ln 5 − ln 1) = (1/2) ln 5. ln 5 comes from forgetting the 1/2 from du = 2x dx, and 2 ln 5 multiplies by 2 instead of dividing. 2/5 is just the value of the function at x = 2.

math1-w10-q14.question: k > 0 and ∫₀ᵏ (2x + 1) dx = 12. What is the value of k?
math1-w10-q14.explanation: ∫₀ᵏ (2x + 1) dx = [x² + x]₀ᵏ = k² + k. k² + k = 12 ⇒ k² + k − 12 = 0 ⇒ (k + 4)(k − 3) = 0 ⇒ k = 3 or −4. Since k > 0, k = 3. Check: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓. −4 breaks the condition k > 0. 2√3 comes from forgetting the integral of + 1 (which is x) and solving k² = 12, and 4 is a sign error in the factors.

math1-w10-q15.question: ∫₀⁵ f(x) dx = 10 and ∫₀² f(x) dx = 4. What is ∫₂⁵ [3f(x) + 2] dx?
math1-w10-q15.explanation: With F an antiderivative, ∫₂⁵ f = F(5) − F(2) = [F(5) − F(0)] − [F(2) − F(0)] = 10 − 4 = 6. Linearity: ∫₂⁵ [3f + 2] dx = 3 · 6 + 2 · (5 − 2) = 18 + 6 = 24. 20 comes from not multiplying the constant 2 by the length of the interval, and 18 drops the + 2 part entirely. 36 = 3 · 10 + 6 wrongly uses the whole ∫₀⁵.

math1-w11-q1.question: An undirected graph has 6 vertices with degrees 2, 3, 3, 2, 4, 2. How many edges does the graph have?
math1-w11-q1.explanation: Degree sum = 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 16 = 2|E|, so |E| = 8. 16 is the degree sum, not the number of edges — each edge is counted twice.

math1-w11-q2.question: Which data structure does BFS mainly use to explore a graph?
math1-w11-q2.explanation: BFS uses a queue (first in, first out), so the nearby (level 1) vertices are processed first, then level 2. A stack is for DFS; a priority queue shows up in algorithms like Dijkstra.

math1-w11-q3.question: How many edges are there in the complete graph K₆?
math1-w11-q3.explanation: One edge between every pair: 6·5/2 = 15. 30 comes from not dividing by 2, i.e. counting every edge twice.

math1-w11-q4.question: Edges of an undirected graph: 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 3–4, 4–5. Run a recursive DFS from vertex 1, visiting neighbours in ascending order. What will the visit order be?
math1-w11-q4.explanation: 1 → smallest neighbour 2 → 2's unvisited neighbour 4 → among 4's neighbours 2, 3, 5 the first unvisited is 3 → all of 3's neighbours are visited, backtrack to 4 → 5. Order 1, 2, 4, 3, 5. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is the BFS order, not DFS.

math1-w11-q5.question: How many 1s will the adjacency matrix of an undirected simple graph with 5 vertices and 7 edges contain?
math1-w11-q5.explanation: An undirected edge i–j puts a 1 in two places in the matrix: A[i][j] and A[j][i]. So 1s = 2 · 7 = 14. 7 comes from forgetting the symmetry; 25 is the number of cells in the whole matrix.

math1-w11-q6.question: Edges of a DAG: A → B, A → C, B → D, C → D, D → E. Which of these is a valid topological order?
math1-w11-q6.explanation: For every edge u → v, u must come first. A, C, B, D, E follows every edge (the order between B and C is free). The first option breaks C → D (D comes before C), the second breaks A → B, and the fourth breaks D → E.

math1-w11-q7.question: The adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is given below. What is the degree of vertex 3?
math1-w11-q7.explanation: In an undirected graph the degree of a vertex = the number of 1s in its row. Row 3: 1, 1, 0, 1, so the degree is 3 (the neighbours of vertex 3 are 1, 2, 4). 4 comes from counting all the cells of the row, including the 0. 10 is the number of 1s in the whole matrix, which is the sum of all degrees (2|E|).

math1-w11-q8.question: Running BFS from a start vertex in an unweighted graph guarantees what?
options: The path with the least total weight in a weighted graph
A path with the minimum number of edges from the start to every reachable vertex
Vertices are always visited in alphabetical order
math1-w11-q8.explanation: BFS goes level by level: first the vertices 1 edge away, then those 2 edges away. So the path by which a vertex is first reached has the minimum number of edges. With weights this guarantee is lost — an algorithm like Dijkstra is needed for that. The visit order depends on the order of the neighbours, and BFS says nothing about whether the graph has a cycle.

math1-w11-q9.question: In what type of graph is a topological order possible?
options: In a directed graph with at least one cycle
Only in a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
math1-w11-q9.explanation: A topological order needs u to come before v for every edge u → v. With a cycle such as A → B → C → A, A would have to come both before and after B — impossible. So only a DAG has a topological order. An undirected graph has no edge directions, so the 'before-after' condition does not even make sense.

math1-w11-q10.question: A complete graph Kₙ has 28 edges. How many vertices does it have?
math1-w11-q10.explanation: Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges: n(n − 1)/2 = 28 ⇒ n(n − 1) = 56 = 8 · 7, so n = 8. 7 vertices give only 7 · 6/2 = 21 edges. 56 is n(n − 1), not n, and 14 = 28/2 misuses the formula.

math1-w11-q11.question: Undirected graph edges: S–A, S–B, A–C, B–C, C–D, D–E, B–F, F–E. Run BFS from S. What is the level of vertex E (minimum number of edges from S)?
math1-w11-q11.explanation: Level 0: S. Level 1: A, B. Level 2: C (from A/B), F (from B). Level 3: D (from C), E (from F). So E is at level 3, path S → B → F → E. 4 comes from following the longer path S → A → C → D → E (thinking like DFS). The level at which BFS first finds a vertex is its minimum distance.

math1-w11-q12.question: Undirected graph edges: A–B, A–D, B–C, B–E, D–E, C–F, E–F, D–G. Run BFS from A, putting neighbours into the queue in alphabetical order and marking each vertex visited as soon as it is first found. What is the visit order?
options: A, B, D, C, E, G, F
A, B, C, F, E, D, G
A, B, D, C, E, F, G
A, B, C, E, D, G, F
math1-w11-q12.explanation: Queue [A]. Remove A: add B, D. Remove B: add C, E (A is visited). Remove D: E is already in the queue, add G. Remove C: add F. E, G, F come out with nothing new. Order: A, B, D, C, E, G, F. 'A, B, C, F, E, D, G' is the DFS order. 'A, B, D, C, E, F, G' puts G after F, although G entered the queue at level 2 through D, while F is at level 3.

math1-w11-q13.question: Which of these degree sequences can NOT belong to any simple undirected graph?
math1-w11-q13.explanation: Handshaking lemma: the sum of degrees = 2|E|, which is always even. (3, 3, 3, 3, 3) has sum 15, which is odd, so such a graph is impossible. All the others exist: (3, 3, 3, 3) = K₄, (2, 2, 2, 2, 2) = a cycle on 5 vertices, and (1, 1, 2, 2) = a path on 4 vertices. Rejecting K₄ or the cycle just because 'all degrees are equal' is the trap.

math1-w11-q14.question: DAG edges: A → C, B → C, C → D, C → E. How many different valid topological orders does this DAG have?
math1-w11-q14.explanation: Both A and B must come before C, and D and E after C. So the order always looks like {A, B} → C → {D, E}. A, B can be arranged in 2 ways and D, E in 2 ways: 2 × 2 = 4 orders (such as A, B, C, D, E and B, A, C, E, D). 2 comes from counting the freedom of only one pair. 6 comes from thinking D or E could also come before C.

math1-w11-q15.question: A simple undirected graph is made by removing 7 edges from the complete graph K₁₀. How many 0s does its 10 × 10 adjacency matrix contain?
math1-w11-q15.explanation: K₁₀ has 10 · 9/2 = 45 edges, so 45 − 7 = 38 remain. An undirected edge puts two 1s in the matrix: 1s = 2 · 38 = 76. There are 100 cells, so 0s = 100 − 76 = 24 (10 on the diagonal + 7 · 2 = 14 from the removed edges). 14 forgets the 10 zeros on the diagonal, 17 = 10 + 7 forgets the symmetry (each edge uses two cells), and 62 = 100 − 38 takes the number of 1s to be the number of edges.

math1-w12-q1.question: How many edges does any tree with 10 vertices have?
math1-w12-q1.explanation: A tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges: 10 − 1 = 9. Even one extra edge would create a cycle. 45 is the number of edges in the complete graph K₁₀.

math1-w12-q2.question: When can Dijkstra's algorithm give a wrong answer?
options: When the graph has negative edge weights
math1-w12-q2.explanation: Once Dijkstra finalizes a vertex it never updates it again, assuming any further path can only be longer. A negative edge breaks this assumption. Dijkstra works fine with cycles and with undirected graphs.

math1-w12-q3.question: Undirected weighted graph: S–A (2), S–B (6), A–B (3), A–C (7), B–C (1). What is the shortest distance from S to C?
math1-w12-q3.explanation: Dijkstra: d(A) = 2; via A, B = 2 + 3 = 5 (< 6); via B, C = 5 + 1 = 6; A to C directly = 9. Shortest S → A → B → C = 6. 7 = S → B → C, and 9 = S → A → C — looking only at the obvious routes is the trap.

math1-w12-q4.question: Edges of a graph: P–Q (1), Q–R (2), P–R (3), R–S (4), Q–S (5), P–S (6). What is the total weight of the minimum spanning tree?
math1-w12-q4.explanation: Kruskal: add P–Q (1), add Q–R (2), P–R (3) forms the cycle P-Q-R so skip it, add R–S (4). That gives 3 edges for 4 vertices: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. 10 comes from also taking the cycle edge (3).

math1-w12-q5.question: When does Kruskal's algorithm skip an edge?
options: When that edge forms a cycle with the edges already chosen
When its weight is the largest
When it connects a new vertex to the tree
math1-w12-q5.explanation: Kruskal looks at edges from cheapest to most expensive and skips only an edge that would form a cycle. Even a heavy edge is taken if it joins two separate components — skipping just by looking at the weight is wrong.

math1-w12-q6.question: Undirected graph: A–B (3), A–C (1), B–C (7), B–D (5), C–D (2), D–E (4), C–E (6). If Prim's algorithm starts from A, in what order will the edges be added?
math1-w12-q6.explanation: Tree {A}: cheapest edge A–C (1). {A, C}: options A–B 3, C–D 2, C–E 6, C–B 7 → C–D (2). {A, C, D}: A–B 3, D–E 4, D–B 5 → A–B (3). Then D–E (4). MST weight 10. The second option is the trap — Prim takes the cheapest edge leaving the whole tree, not just A's edges.

math1-w12-q7.question: A connected graph has 8 vertices and 12 edges. At least how many edges must be removed to get a spanning tree?
math1-w12-q7.explanation: A tree on 8 vertices has exactly 8 − 1 = 7 edges. So 12 − 7 = 5 edges must be removed (each removed edge breaks a cycle). 4 = 12 − 8 comes from assuming a tree has n edges. 7 is the number of edges left in the spanning tree, not the number removed.

math1-w12-q8.question: Which algorithm is designed to find the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices of a weighted graph at once?
math1-w12-q8.explanation: Floyd-Warshall finds the shortest distances for all pairs at once, in roughly n³ steps. Kruskal and Prim build a minimum spanning tree, not shortest paths — the path between two vertices in an MST need not be the shortest. BFS only gives minimum-edge paths in an unweighted graph.

math1-w12-q9.question: Both Prim and Kruskal are run on a connected weighted undirected graph. What is true about the MSTs they give?
options: Which one is lighter depends on Prim's start vertex
Both always have the same total weight
math1-w12-q9.explanation: Both algorithms give a minimum spanning tree, and the minimum weight is a single number — so the total weight is always the same. If some edges have equal weights the two may pick different edges (the tree can differ), but the weight does not change. Prim's start vertex only changes the order in which edges are added, not the final weight.

math1-w12-q10.question: Directed weighted graph edges: S → A (4), S → B (1), B → A (2), A → C (1), B → C (5), C → D (3), A → D (6). What is the shortest distance from S to D?
math1-w12-q10.explanation: Dijkstra: d(S) = 0; from S, d(B) = 1, d(A) = 4. Finalise B: d(A) = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3, d(C) = 6. Finalise A (3): d(C) = min(6, 3 + 1) = 4, d(D) = 9. Finalise C (4): d(D) = min(9, 4 + 3) = 7. Path S → B → A → C → D = 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 7. 8 = S → A → C → D (taking the direct S → A as final), and 9 = S → B → C → D or S → B → A → D.

math1-w12-q11.question: A connected undirected simple graph has 9 vertices and 9 edges. What is true about it?
options: Such a graph is not possible
The graph has exactly one cycle
math1-w12-q11.explanation: A spanning tree of the connected graph has 9 − 1 = 8 edges. The graph has one extra edge, and adding one edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle. So there is exactly one cycle. 'No cycle' would be true only with 8 edges (a tree). The graph is possible too, for example a single cycle through all 9 vertices.

math1-w12-q12.question: Undirected weighted graph: A–B (2), A–C (5), B–C (1), B–D (4), C–D (1), D–E (3), C–E (6). What are the shortest distance and path from A to E?
math1-w12-q12.explanation: Dijkstra from A: d(B) = 2, d(C) = min(5, 2 + 1) = 3, d(D) = min(2 + 4, 3 + 1) = 4, d(E) = min(3 + 6, 4 + 3) = 7. Path A → B → C → D → E = 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 7 — more edges, but less weight. A → B → D → E and A → B → C → E both give 9; stopping at a route with fewer edges is the trap. A → C → E = 11 uses only direct edges.

math1-w12-q13.question: Graph edges: P–Q (2), P–R (3), Q–R (2), Q–S (4), R–S (4), R–T (5), S–T (1), Q–T (6). What is the total weight of the minimum spanning tree?
math1-w12-q13.explanation: Kruskal (in weight order): add S–T (1); add P–Q (2); add Q–R (2); P–R (3) makes the cycle P-Q-R, skip; add Q–S (4) — now {P, Q, R} and {S, T} are joined. 5 vertices need 4 edges: 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9. R–S (4) also weighs 4, but it would now make a cycle — in a tie take either one, the weight stays 9. 12 comes from taking P–R (3) without the cycle check, and 10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 takes P–R (3) instead of the cheaper Q–R (2).

math1-w12-q14.question: Directed weighted graph edges: S → A (2), S → B (4), B → A (−3), A → C (3), B → C (4), C → D (2), A → D (6). One edge is negative, but there is no negative cycle. What is the true shortest distance from S to D, and along which path?
options: Not defined, because the graph has a negative edge
math1-w12-q14.explanation: With a negative edge, check the routes the Bellman-Ford way (in the order S, B, A, C, D): d(B) = 4, d(A) = min(2, 4 + (−3)) = 1, d(C) = min(1 + 3, 4 + 4) = 4, d(D) = min(4 + 2, 1 + 6) = 6. Path S → B → A → C → D = 4 − 3 + 3 + 2 = 6. 7 = S → A → C → D — what you get if you treat d(A) = 2 as final too early (the Dijkstra trap with a negative edge). 8 = S → A → D. A shortest distance is undefined only when there is a negative cycle; here there is no cycle at all.

math1-w12-q15.question: Undirected graph edges: A–B (3), B–C (4), A–C (x), C–D (2), B–D (6), where x > 0. For which value of x is the total weight of the minimum spanning tree exactly 8?
math1-w12-q15.explanation: An MST on 4 vertices has 3 edges. C–D (2) and A–B (3) always get in (cheapest, no cycle). The third edge joins C to {A, B}: A–C (x) or B–C (4), whichever is cheaper. So the MST weight = 2 + 3 + min(x, 4). This is 8 when min(x, 4) = 3, i.e. x = 3. x = 2 gives weight 7, and x = 4 or 5 keeps the weight at 9 using B–C (4) — once x ≥ 4, x has no effect at all.
